blocks.body:
A taxi fare depends on the distance driven; the temperature depends on the time of day. In each case one quantity determines another, and a function is the mathematical name for such a rule.

This lesson defines functions, reads their properties from graphs, moves graphs around, and shows how functions are combined and undone.

blocks.title: Function
blocks.body:
Let $A$ and $B$ be sets. A function $f$ from $A$ to $B$, written $f\colon A \to B$, is a rule that assigns to each element $x \in A$ exactly one element $f(x) \in B$. The set $A$ is the domain of $f$ and $B$ is its codomain. The set of values actually taken,
$$f(A) = \{ f(x) : x \in A \},$$
is the range (or image) of $f$.

In short: every input gets an output, and no input gets two.

blocks.title: Domain, range and graph
blocks.body:
When a function is given by a formula and nothing else is said, its domain is all real $x$ for which the formula makes sense: every $x \ne 2$ for $\dfrac{1}{x - 2}$, and $x \ge 1$ for $\sqrt{x - 1}$, since negative numbers have no real square root.

The range is often harder. For $h(x) = x^2 + 1$, every value is at least $1$ because $x^2 \ge 0$, and every $y \ge 1$ is reached, at $x = \sqrt{y - 1}$. So the range is $[1, \infty)$. Finding a range means asking for which $y$ the equation $f(x) = y$ has a solution in the domain.

The graph of $f$ is the set of points $(x, f(x))$ with $x$ in the domain. One output per input means that every vertical line meets a graph at most once; so the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ is not a graph, though its upper half is the graph of $\sqrt{1 - x^2}$.

Begin a sketch with a table of values. For $f(x) = x^2 - 2x - 3$:
$$\begin{array}{c|ccccccc} x & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline f(x) & 5 & 0 & -3 & -4 & -3 & 0 & 5 \end{array}$$
The values fall and then rise, symmetrically about $x = 1$, with zeros at $-1$ and $3$. Indeed $f(x) = (x + 1)(x - 3) = (x - 1)^2 - 4$: a parabola with lowest point $(1, -4)$.

blocks.title: Reading a graph
blocks.body:
Several properties have both an algebraic definition and a picture.

- $f$ is increasing on an interval if $x_1 < x_2$ implies $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ there: the graph rises from left to right. Decreasing: $x_1 < x_2$ implies $f(x_1) > f(x_2)$.
- A zero of $f$ is an $x$ with $f(x) = 0$, where the graph meets the $x$-axis.
- $f$ is even if $f(-x) = f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain: the graph is symmetric in the $y$-axis, as for $x^2$ and $|x|$.
- $f$ is odd if $f(-x) = -f(x)$ for all $x$ in the domain: the graph is unchanged by a half turn about the origin, as for $x^3$ and $1/x$.

Most functions are neither, but if the domain is symmetric about $0$, then
$$f(x) = \frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2} + \frac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2}$$
writes $f$ as an even function plus an odd one. For instance $x^2 - 2x - 3$ has even part $x^2 - 3$ and odd part $-2x$.

blocks.title: Moving and stretching graphs
blocks.body:
Suppose you know the graph of $y = f(x)$. With $h, k$ real and $a > 0$:

1. $y = f(x) + k$: shift up by $k$.
2. $y = f(x - h)$: shift right by $h$.
3. $y = a f(x)$: stretch vertically by the factor $a$.
4. $y = f(x/a)$: stretch horizontally by the factor $a$.
5. $y = -f(x)$: reflect in the $x$-axis; $y = f(-x)$: reflect in the $y$-axis.

Rule 2 surprises people: a minus sign moves the graph right. The reason is that $f(x - h)$ takes at $x_0 + h$ the value $f(x_0)$, which $f$ took at $x_0$.

Completing the square uses these rules. Since $2x^2 - 12x + 19 = 2(x - 3)^2 + 1$, the graph of $y = 2x^2 - 12x + 19$ is the parabola $y = x^2$ stretched vertically by $2$, moved $3$ right and $1$ up. Its lowest point is $(3, 1)$ and its range is $[1, \infty)$.

blocks.title: Composition and inverse
blocks.body:
If $f\colon A \to B$ and $g\colon B \to C$, the composition $g \circ f\colon A \to C$ is defined by $(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x))$: first apply $f$, then $g$.

A function $g\colon B \to A$ is an inverse of $f\colon A \to B$ if $g(f(x)) = x$ for every $x \in A$ and $f(g(y)) = y$ for every $y \in B$. When it exists it is written $f^{-1}$.

blocks.title: Composing and undoing
blocks.body:
Order matters in composition. With $f(x) = x + 1$ and $g(x) = x^2$, $(g \circ f)(x) = (x + 1)^2$ but $(f \circ g)(x) = x^2 + 1$; at $x = 1$ these are $4$ and $2$.

A function composed with itself can surprise. Let $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{1 - x}$ for $x \ne 1$. For $x \ne 0, 1$,
$$f(f(x)) = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{1 - x}} = \frac{x - 1}{x}, \qquad f(f(f(x))) = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{x - 1}{x}} = x.$$
Three applications of $f$ bring every number except $0$ and $1$ back to where it started ($f(0) = 1$ and $f(1)$ is undefined).

To undo $f$, different inputs must give different outputs, and every element of $B$ must be an output. So: $f$ is injective (one-to-one) if $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ implies $x_1 = x_2$; for a real function, every horizontal line meets the graph at most once. $f$ is surjective (onto) if its range is all of $B$. A function that is both is a bijection.

blocks.title: Inverses exist exactly for bijections
blocks.body: A function $f\colon A \to B$ has an inverse if and only if it is a bijection. The inverse is then unique. For real functions, the graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Suppose $g$ is an inverse of $f$. If $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$, then $x_1 = g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)) = x_2$, so $f$ is injective. Every $y \in B$ equals $f(g(y))$, so $f$ is surjective.

Conversely, let $f$ be a bijection. Each $y \in B$ is $f(x)$ for some $x \in A$ (surjectivity), and for only one (injectivity); let $g(y)$ be that $x$. Then $f(g(y)) = y$ by construction, and $g(f(x)) = x$ because $x$ is the only input with output $f(x)$.

If $g$ and $g'$ are both inverses, then for every $y \in B$, $g(y) = g\big(f(g'(y))\big) = g'(y)$. So the inverse is unique.

Finally, $(p, q)$ is on the graph of $f$ exactly when $q = f(p)$, that is, when $p = f^{-1}(q)$, that is, when $(q, p)$ is on the graph of $f^{-1}$. Swapping the coordinates of every point is reflection in the line $y = x$.

blocks.title: Domain, range and inverse of a fraction
blocks.body: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$. Find its domain and range, and a formula for $f^{-1}$.
blocks.solution:
The formula makes sense except at $x = 3$, so the domain is $\mathbb R \setminus \{3\}$.

For the range, solve $f(x) = y$:
$$y(x - 3) = 2x + 1 \iff x(y - 2) = 3y + 1.$$
If $y \ne 2$ this gives $x = \dfrac{3y + 1}{y - 2}$, which is not $3$ (otherwise $3y - 6 = 3y + 1$), so it lies in the domain. If $y = 2$ the equation reads $0 = 7$: impossible. So the range is $\mathbb R \setminus \{2\}$.

Each $y \ne 2$ comes from exactly one $x$, so $f$ is a bijection from $\mathbb R \setminus \{3\}$ to $\mathbb R \setminus \{2\}$ with
$$f^{-1}(y) = \frac{3y + 1}{y - 2}.$$
Test: $f(4) = 9$ and $f^{-1}(9) = 28/7 = 4$.

In pictures, $f(x) = 2 + \dfrac{7}{x - 3}$ is $7/x$ moved $3$ right and $2$ up.

blocks.title: Counting solutions with a graph
blocks.body: For each real number $c$, how many real solutions does $|x^2 - 4| = c$ have?

blocks.title: A functional equation
blocks.body: Find all functions $f\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ such that $f(x) + 2f(1 - x) = x^2$ for every real $x$.
blocks.solution:
Replacing $x$ by $1 - x$ gives a second equation in the same unknowns $f(x)$ and $f(1 - x)$:
$$f(1 - x) + 2f(x) = (1 - x)^2.$$
Multiply it by $2$ and subtract the original; the $f(1 - x)$ terms cancel:
$$3f(x) = 2(1 - x)^2 - x^2 = x^2 - 4x + 2, \qquad f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4x + 2}{3}.$$
So any solution must be this function. Check that it works: since $(1 - x)^2 - 4(1 - x) + 2 = x^2 + 2x - 1$,
$$f(x) + 2f(1 - x) = \frac{(x^2 - 4x + 2) + 2(x^2 + 2x - 1)}{3} = x^2.$$
So there is exactly one such function. The check matters: derived conditions are necessary, not always sufficient.

blocks.body:
- $f^{-1}(x)$ is the inverse function, not $1/f(x)$: for $f(x) = 2x$, $f^{-1}(x) = x/2$ but $1/f(x) = 1/(2x)$.
- $y = f(x - 3)$ is the graph moved right, not left; $g \circ f$ means apply $f$ first.
- Whether an inverse exists depends on the domain. $x^2$ on $\mathbb R$ is not injective, as $(-2)^2 = 2^2$; on $[0, \infty)$ it is a bijection onto $[0, \infty)$ with inverse $\sqrt y$. That is why $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|$.
- The domain is part of the function: $\dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1}$ and $x + 1$ differ at $x = 1$, where the first is undefined.

A sequence is a function on the positive integers; the simplest ones are in [[ap-gp]]. The great non-algebraic families are [[exp-log]] and [[trig]], each a bijection after a suitable restriction. Calculus starts with what a function does near a point: [[limits]] and [[continuity]].

Finding an unknown function from an equation it satisfies is an olympiad topic of its own ([[real-functional-eq]], [[integer-functional-eq]]). Bijections are the basic tool of [[counting]], and the functions of linear algebra are the [[linear-maps]].

1. Find the domain and range of $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^2}$ and describe its graph.
2. Show that $f(x) = x^3 + x$ is injective on $\mathbb R$. (Hint: factor $f(a) - f(b)$.)
3. For $f(x) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x - 1}$, compute $f(f(x))$. What does the answer tell you about $f^{-1}$?
4. Find all functions $f\colon \mathbb R \setminus \{0\} \to \mathbb R$ with $f(x) + 2f(1/x) = 3x$.
